content.question: In Episode 3 the instructor partitioned the calculator screen into three main vertical parts. Which of the following accurately describes those three parts?

options.text: Header (title), calculation display box, and the numbers/operators area.
Toolbar, navigation drawer, and footer action bar.
Status bar, notification pane, and settings panel.
A single ConstraintLayout with three overlapping fragments.

content.explanation: The screen is divided into three vertical boxes: the heading (text view), the calculation/display box, and the numbers+operators area — exactly as the instructor described.
hints: He named them heading, calculation box, and number/operator box.
This was not about toolbars or system panels.
Numbers and operators were later split into nested parts.

content.question: To implement the number pad, what nesting approach did the instructor use so that number rows appear horizontally while the overall pad stacks vertically?

options.text: One vertical LinearLayout that contains multiple horizontal LinearLayouts; each horizontal LinearLayout holds a row of buttons.
Several FrameLayouts layered with Z-index to simulate rows.
A single horizontal LinearLayout with layout_weight to wrap rows automatically.
Use a GridLayout with fixed row counts only; nesting wasn't used.

content.explanation: He created a vertical parent for the pad and inside it added horizontal LinearLayouts for each row. This yields rows that are horizontal while the pad itself stacks vertically.
hints: He copied a horizontal group and pasted it multiple times for extra rows.
He explicitly set orientation='horizontal' on the row containers.
The transcript shows repeating horizontal blocks inside a vertical area.

content.question: Which widget did the instructor prefer for the calculator buttons to allow easier styling and consistent behavior across API levels?

options.text: android.widget.Button (the platform Button).
ImageButton only, since calculator buttons must be icons.
androidx.appcompat.widget.AppCompatButton for reliable styling control.
TextView with clickable='true' because it avoids button styling issues.

content.explanation: He used AppCompatButton when creating numeric buttons to easily set size, background color, and font across devices. AppCompat offers consistent styling support.
hints: He typed 'app compact button I am giving 50 dp'.
The choice was about consistent styling across API levels.
He didn't use TextView hacks for all numeric keys.

content.question: What did the instructor change when he realized the buttons needed space around them: padding or margin, and why?

options.text: He used padding because padding creates space outside the view between siblings.
He used margin to create space between sibling views because margin affects a view's outside spacing.
He used layout_weight instead of margin or padding to create breathing room.
He removed all spacing—buttons naturally space themselves in LinearLayout.

content.explanation: He opted for margin (e.g., margin 10dp or 5dp) to space the buttons apart; margins control external spacing between sibling views.
hints: He said 'not padding instead of padding let us go with margin.'
Margin affects outside spacing; padding affects inside content area.
Weights were not introduced as the spacing solution.

content.question: Why did the instructor enable 'blueprint' or design preview when building the calculator screen?

options.text: To get an idea of placement and spacing visually while arranging components before running the app.
To force the app to build faster by caching layouts.
To automatically generate vector drawables for the UI.
To convert LinearLayouts into ConstraintLayouts automatically.

content.explanation: The blueprint/design preview helps visualize placements and spacing so you know where to position components before running the app.
hints: He said blueprint gives an idea of placement we are working right now.
It's a visual aid, not a build speed tool.
No automatic conversion of layouts happens.

content.question: What font and size did the instructor choose for the heading in Episode 3?

options.text: Poppins Medium at 30dp.
Roboto Regular at 12sp.
System Default at 24sp.
Arial Bold at 40dp.

content.explanation: He set the heading font to Poppins Medium and increased the size to 30 (noting 30 dp as the chosen size for the title).
hints: He used Poppins medium and 'increase the size of it that is size 30 db'.
The heading was bold and centered.
Other options are not mentioned in the transcript.

content.question: Why did the instructor increase number button sizes from 50 to 60dp during the demo?

options.text: To create more space for padding and improve usability when tapped.
Because smaller sizes are not allowed on Android.
To break the layout intentionally for demonstration.
To ensure the buttons are invisible until pressed.

content.explanation: He increased the button size to give more space for padding and margins, improving the visual layout and tappable area.
hints: He said there was enough space and increased the size to 60dp.
Larger buttons improve touch targets.
This was a design decision, not a platform requirement.

content.question: Which attribute did the instructor set to center the heading horizontally on the screen?

options.text: android:gravity='center' or center_horizontal on the TextView.
android:layout_margin='0dp' only.
android:paddingLeft='50dp' to push it centrally.
Use a separate ImageView behind the text to fake centering.

content.explanation: He used center gravity (center or center_horizontal) on the TextView to align the heading horizontally.
hints: He said 'put it into centre gravity centre horizontal'.
Gravity aligns content inside the view.
Margins or padding are not the intended centering technique here.

content.question: Why did the instructor change the calculation box background from black to a named resource like 'text_blue'?

options.text: To reuse a named color across the app and keep consistent branding rather than hardcoding inline hex values.
Because black is not supported on TextViews.
To convert the TextView into an ImageView.
To automatically make the box clickable.

content.explanation: He replaced an ad-hoc black value with a named resource (like text_blue) so it can be reused and maintain consistent visuals across components.
hints: He moved away from hard-coded colors into resource values.
Named colors live in res/values/colors.xml.
This is about reusability, not support or click behavior.

content.question: When creating rows of number buttons, what small change ensured consistent spacing between buttons?

options.text: Applying a margin of 5dp (or 10dp) to each button to separate siblings.
Setting android:visibility='gone' on alternate buttons.
Using an extra ConstraintLayout for each button.
Setting the button text to an empty string.

content.explanation: He used margin (5dp or 10dp) on buttons to create breathing room between them, improving layout clarity and touch targets.
hints: He chose margin over padding for outside spacing.
Margins were copied when he pasted rows of buttons.
This was a spacing, not visibility, change.
